newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong ponders reunion with China without Deng.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong ponders reunion with China without Deng.

text.p: British and Chinese flags flew at half mast over Hong Kong on Thursday as residents warily pondered a future without Deng Xiaoping with the handover to China just months away.
Deng, 92 according to the Western calendar, died of respiratory failure late on Wednesday and Hong Kong's sensitive antennae had twitched for days to rumours about the patriarch's health.

Newspapers delayed early editions to trumpet the news in banner headlines. Radio and television suspended normal programming to examine the implications for Hong Kong's 6.3 million people bracing for the handover of the British colony.

For China, more than a century and a half of humiliation at the hands of a foreign occupying power comes to an end when the British depart at midnight on June 30, 1997, and Hong Kong once again becomes a part of China.
Hong Kong people's views about the future were deeply divided.
Government officials and pro-Beijing politicians, united for once, confidently forecast no change in the countdown to the handover.

"From what we can see, since 1992, 1993, Deng Xiaoping has not said anything more in relation to Hong Kong. I think it (his death) should not affect Hong Kong's transition," said Tsang Yok-sing, chairman of the pro-Beijing Democratic Alliance for the Betterment of Hong Kong (DAB).
Hong Kong's most senior civil servant Anson Chan agreed, saying: "I don't think it will affect the smooth transition".

But the influential South China Morning Post newspaper painted a worrying picture of Hong Kong's future now the mastermind of the reforms which transformed China into an emerging economic powerhouse has gone to meet Mao.
"Although Deng's death is unlikely to result in a major immediate policy shift over Hong Kong, changes in the corridors of power in Beijing will spill over into the territory."
"The hidden source of friction within the Chinese hierarchy over Hong Kong policy is bound to erupt in the post-Deng era.
"The long-standing bickering over whether Beijing's Hong Kong policy is too hard or too soft -- or so-called 'leftist' or 'rightist' -- is set to intensify and break into the open."
As it result, it said, Beijing may now adopt a tougher stance over Hong Kong.
But Hong Kong's notoriously volatile stock market confounded those who feared a knee-jerk fall by swiftly shaking off an early decline to move higher in morning trade.
Deng will now never achieve his ambition of seeing Hong Kong return to the fold.
But his ghost will no doubt hover over the ceremonies when the British flag is furled for the last time and China's red flag rises over Hong Kong.
It was Deng who was credited with formulating the "one country, two systems" formula which made it possible for the British to agree to return Hong Kong to communist China.
China promised Hong Kong's freedoms and its capitalist lifestyle would prevail for 50 years.
Hong Kong money and Deng's economic reforms have narrowed the gulf between Hong Kong and southern China, sweeping away fears that Hong Kong would drown in a bottomless pit of poverty.
Instead, both Hong Kong and China prospered in tandem and few now fear Deng's demise would allow the hardliners back to reverse the reforms and send the bamboo curtain crashing down again.
